modern: Are you angry with the man whose armpits stink? Are you angry with the man whose mouth smells foul? What good will this anger do you? He has such a mouth, he has such armpits: such an odour must necessarily come from such things: but the man has reason, it will be said, and he is able, if he takes the trouble, to discover how he gives offence; congratulations on your discovery. Well then, you have reason too: by your rational faculty stir up his rational faculty; show him his error, warn him. For if he listens, you will cure him, and there is no need for anger. Neither tragic actor nor whore.
original: Art thou angry with him whose armpits stink? art thou angry with him whose mouth smells foul? What good will this anger do thee? He has such a mouth, he has such armpits: it is necessary that such an emanation must come from such things: but the man has reason, it will be said, and he is able, if he takes pains, to discover wherein he offends; I wish thee well of thy discovery. Well then, and thou hast reason: by thy rational faculty stir up his rational faculty; show him his error, admonish him. For if he listens, thou wilt cure him, and there is no need of anger. [Neither tragic actor nor whore.]

notification_original: Art thou angry with him whose armpits stink? art thou angry with him whose mouth smells foul? What good will this anger do thee?

explained.summary:
Getting angry at someone because their breath or armpits smell achieves nothing. That’s just how they are. You might say they have reason and could work out that they’re offending people. Well, so do you: use yours to help them see it. Tell them, kindly. If they listen, the problem is solved and anger never came into it.

The cryptic last line seems to mean: don’t make a theatrical scene, and don’t fawn over them either.
explained.today: The modern version is the colleague who chews loudly or the flatmate who never empties the bin. Seething silently or complaining about them to others helps no one. A quiet, friendly word usually does.
